promptText: What is the primary weakness of reactive (ReAct-style) planning compared to plan-and-execute?
options: It has no global view of the goal and can wander, repeat work, or lose track of the objective over long horizons
It cannot be used with tool-calling APIs at all
It always costs more tokens than plan-and-execute on every task
It requires a fully hand-encoded STRIPS-style domain model before it can run
explanation: Reactive planning reasons about only the next step at a time with no separate planning phase, so it naturally adapts to surprises but lacks a global view of the goal over long-horizon tasks.

promptText: Why must a generated plan be validated with deterministic code before a single step executes?
options: Because it makes the JSON output shorter and cheaper to store
Because it is required syntax for calling any LLM API
Because it is generated by a probabilistic model and can reference nonexistent tools, invalid step ordering, or exceed current permissions
Because validation is the only way to reduce the plan's token count before execution
explanation: A plan is a probabilistic model's output and cannot be trusted to self-police; deterministic validation checks tool existence, argument shape, dependency ordering, and permissions before any real-world action occurs.

promptText: What specifically should trigger a re-plan during execution?
options: Any step that takes longer than the average step in the plan
Whenever the plan has grown beyond three or four steps
A step failing outright, or a step succeeding but its real observation invalidating an assumption the rest of the plan depended on
Whenever the token cost of the conversation exceeds the model's average per-request cost
explanation: A re-plan is needed when a step errors, or when a step's real result diverges from what downstream steps assumed — not for ordinary expected variation the plan already accounts for.

promptText: If a plan step succeeds with probability p per attempt and each attempt costs c tokens/dollars, what is the approximate expected cost to complete that step via naive retry-until-success?
options: c / p
c * p
c + p
c raised to the power p
explanation: Expected cost of retry-until-success is roughly c / p; when p is low, this grows quickly, which is the justification for a bounded-retry-then-escalate policy instead of unbounded retrying.

promptText: What does "grounding" mean specifically in the context of agent planning?
options: Converting the plan into a JSON array instead of free text
Basing the plan on real, current retrieved context — the actual tool list, actual system state, actual constraints — rather than trusting the model's prior alone
Caching a validated plan for reuse across similar future goals
Reducing the number of tokens the planning prompt consumes
explanation: An ungrounded planner will confidently generate a plausible-sounding but fictional plan drawn from training-data averages rather than the actual environment; grounding fixes this by feeding real state into the planning step.

promptText: Why would you represent a plan as a DAG (directed acyclic graph) rather than a flat ordered list?
options: DAGs are the only format LLMs are capable of generating reliably
A DAG makes each step's actual dependencies explicit, enabling parallel execution of independent steps and trivial cycle detection during validation
A DAG format is mandated by most tool-calling APIs
Representing a plan as a DAG eliminates the need for a plan validator
explanation: A flat list forces a single total ordering even when steps have no real dependency on each other; a DAG exposes true dependencies for parallelism, cycle detection, and critical-path analysis.

promptText: Compare a ReWOO/LLMCompiler-style decoupled planning approach to interleaved ReAct-style planning. What does decoupling actually buy you?
options: It guarantees the plan is mathematically optimal before execution begins
Lower total latency and cost through parallel execution of independent steps and fewer full reasoning calls, at the cost of losing per-step adaptivity
It removes the need for a plan validator entirely since the executor is non-LLM
It eliminates the possibility of a step ever failing at runtime
explanation: Decoupled approaches generate the whole plan upfront with placeholder variables and let a non-LLM executor run independent steps concurrently, cutting cost and latency but requiring a separate repair path if an early result invalidates a later step's premise.

promptText: Why is plan repair often preferable to a full replan when a divergence occurs?
options: Repair guarantees the corrected plan will be correct on the next attempt
Repair is always cheaper than a full replan regardless of how large the divergence is
Repair produces a minimal revision while preserving already-completed steps and their side effects, making it cheaper and safer when the divergence is local
Repair removes the need to re-validate the plan before continuing execution
explanation: Plan repair patches only the remaining steps while treating completed steps as fixed history, avoiding redundant re-derivation and preventing re-execution of side effects that already succeeded; a full replan is warranted only when the divergence undermines the plan's fundamental approach.

promptText: What is the key distinction between an "information-gathering" plan step and an "execution" plan step?
options: Information-gathering steps never call a tool, while execution steps always do
Information-gathering steps reduce the agent's uncertainty about the world before a consequential action; execution steps actually change the world or produce the deliverable
Information-gathering steps are always the first step in any plan by definition
There is no meaningful distinction; both categories should be validated identically
explanation: Conflating the two is a common planning bug — treating a status-check step as optional under an assumed state is planning under a false sense of full observability.

promptText: Why does self-consistency (sampling multiple candidate plans and checking for agreement) improve planning reliability?
options: It guarantees the majority plan is provably correct
It eliminates the need for a plan validator downstream
A single generated plan might be an unlucky draw; convergence across independent samples is itself a signal of higher confidence than any one sample alone
It reduces the total token cost of planning compared to generating one plan
explanation: Self-consistency is a cheap, model-agnostic way to raise plan reliability at the cost of extra generation calls, most valuable at decision points where a wrong plan is expensive.

promptText: How does "plan degeneration" differ from the single-step divergence detection described earlier in the planning loop?
options: Plan degeneration is just another name for a single tool call throwing an exception

Divergence detection catches one bad step; plan degeneration is the accumulation of several individually-reasonable repairs into a collectively-wrong trajectory, with no single step being an obvious error
Plan degeneration only happens in Tree-of-Thought planning, never in Plan-and-Execute
Plan degeneration is detected automatically by the same validator that checks tool existence
explanation: Plan degeneration is harder to catch than a single failed step because no individual repair trips an error; it requires periodically re-checking the current trajectory against the original goal statement directly.

promptText: Why should plan generation and plan validation/execution be kept as separate architectural responsibilities in a Java/Spring agent codebase?
options: Because Spring AI's ChatClient API technically forbids combining them in one class
Generation is inherently probabilistic and belongs to the model, while validation and execution must be deterministic and auditable; mixing them makes the system nearly impossible to unit-test
Separation is purely a performance optimization with no testing benefit
Because validation logic must run on a different JVM than the model call
explanation: You cannot deterministically unit-test 'did the executor correctly handle a step failure' when plan generation and execution are entangled in the same non-deterministic call — keeping them separate is the core design instinct this chapter stresses.

promptText: A production agent has started taking 20-30 model calls to complete tasks that should take 5, and cost has become unpredictable. What is the most likely root cause, and what is the correct first diagnostic step?
options: The model's context window is too large; the fix is to switch to a smaller-context model

This is almost always a high replanning rate traceable to poor tool descriptions, insufficient grounding context, or missing attempt budgets; the first step is instrumenting and logging every plan, validation failure, and replanning trigger with its cause
The team should immediately switch from Plan-and-Execute to reactive planning to reduce call count
The issue is inherent to LLM agents and cannot be diagnosed without retraining the model
explanation: Runaway call counts are almost always a symptom of a high replanning rate; the fix starts with instrumentation to see the distribution of failure reasons rather than guessing, then remediating tool descriptions, grounding, and budgets accordingly.

promptText: Why is it insufficient for an executor to check a step's preconditions only at plan-generation time rather than immediately before that step executes?
options: Precondition checks at generation time always cost more tokens than checking at execution time

Environment state can change between when the plan was generated and when a later step actually runs, and the step may execute without throwing any error even though the world has moved on — making this failure mode silent unless deliberately re-checked
Preconditions never change once a plan has been generated, so this scenario cannot actually occur
Modern LLM APIs automatically re-verify preconditions before every tool call
explanation: The longer a plan runs, the more time passes for the world to change underneath it; re-verifying load-bearing preconditions against fresh observations right before each step executes is the only way to catch this class of divergence, since the step itself may succeed mechanically against stale assumptions.

promptText: When parallelizing independent steps of a plan represented as a DAG, what kind of conflict will the DAG's data-dependency edges alone fail to catch?
options: Two steps that both read the same data source without writing anything
Two steps that share no data dependency in the graph but both write to the same external resource, creating a side-effect conflict invisible in the DAG unless explicitly annotated
Any two steps assigned consecutive step numbers in the plan
A step that has more than one direct predecessor in the graph
explanation: Data dependency (one step's output feeding another's input) is visible in a DAG, but side-effect dependency — two steps mutating the same external state with no data link between them — is invisible unless flagged explicitly, a distinction most engineers miss.
